The move was described by legal experts as an attempted assertion of an unconstitutional impoundment power not seen since Richard Nixon. The Constitution's Article I explicitly vests the power of the purse in Congress. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order within 24 hours. OMB Director Russell Vought publicly stated in June 2025 that impoundment was certainly not off the table. The administration's sustained effort to cancel, freeze, and redirect congressionally appropriated funds throughout 2025 generated dozens of lawsuits; courts largely blocked the moves but the legal battle was ongoing as of August 2026.

sources.title: White House Eyes Rarely Used Power to Override Congress on Spending

title: Mass Pardons for All 1,500+ January 6 Capitol Rioters
synopsis: On January 21, 2025, his second day in office, Trump signed an executive grant of clemency covering all 1,500-plus individuals charged in connection with the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack — including convicted leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys who had been found guilty of seditious conspiracy for orchestrating violent plots to stop the peaceful transfer of power. The pardons upended what prosecutors called the largest prosecution in Justice Department history, freeing individuals caught on camera assaulting police officers, resulting in more than 100 officers being injured. Among those freed were individuals who had received sentences of up to 18 years. Critics noted the pardons directly rewarded participants in an insurrection Trump had incited. The move was widely interpreted as Trump signaling that political violence carried out in his name would be shielded from legal consequence, chilling future prosecution of political violence and undermining democratic norms.

title: DOJ Fires Career Prosecutors Who Worked on Trump Investigations
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, Acting Attorney General James McHenry fired more than a dozen career Justice Department prosecutors who had worked on Special Counsel Jack Smith's two federal criminal investigations of Donald Trump. McHenry stated they could not be trusted to faithfully implement the President's agenda because of their role in prosecuting Trump — a rationale that explicitly made professional loyalty to the president, rather than the law, the criterion for employment. Career DOJ veterans described the firings as an egregious violation of norms designed to insulate law enforcement from political manipulation and preserve the independence of federal prosecution. The firings came alongside the reassignment of the department's most senior career official and followed Trump's first-day pardon of January 6 defendants. Legal scholars warned the combination effectively dismantled the DOJ's historic independence and transformed it into an instrument of personal presidential power.

title: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause
synopsis: In late January and early February 2025, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox from the National Labor Relations Board, Cathy Harris from the Merit Systems Protection Board, and Alvaro Bedoya and Rebecca Kelly Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission — all without cause, in direct violation of federal statutes that permit removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance in office. These multi-member independent agencies were created by Congress with for-cause removal protections upheld by the Supreme Court for 90 years under Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). Acting Solicitor General Sarah Harris formally informed Congress in February 2025 that the DOJ would no longer defend the constitutional validity of these protections. The Supreme Court, in a 6-3 emergency stay in Trump v. Wilcox (May 2025), allowed the firings to proceed pending full review — with Justice Kagan's dissent warning the majority had allowed Trump to overrule Humphrey's by fiat and signaled the eventual overturn of a foundational check on presidential power.

title: Executive Orders Targeting Law Firms That Opposed Trump
synopsis: In March 2025, Trump signed executive orders against at least two major law firms that had represented clients opposing him or participated in his prosecutions. On March 6, an order against Perkins Coie — which had represented Hillary Clinton in 2016 — suspended the security clearances of all firm employees, directed federal agencies to terminate contracts, and launched a government-wide investigation of large law firms' diversity practices. On March 14, a nearly identical order targeted Paul Weiss because a former partner had brought a pro bono suit related to January 6 defendants. The orders blocked firm employees from entering federal buildings and directed agencies to require contractors to disclose any business with the targeted firms. A federal judge temporarily blocked the Perkins Coie order. Legal experts condemned both orders as a chilling use of executive power to punish lawyers for their clients' identities and associations, threatening access to justice and the independence of the legal system from political retaliation.

title: Trump Deploys Marines and Federalized National Guard to Los Angeles Over Protests
synopsis: On June 7, 2025, Trump issued a presidential memorandum deploying approximately 2,000 California National Guard troops — taken from Governor Gavin Newsom's control against his explicit objections — plus 700 active-duty Marines to Los Angeles in response to protests against ICE immigration raids. The administration labeled the protests a possible form of rebellion against the authority of the U.S. government. Newsom called the deployment unnecessary and counterproductive. Federal Judge Charles Breyer issued a temporary restraining order on June 12, ruling Trump had failed to meet the legal prerequisites under 10 U.S.C. 12406. A federal judge later ruled the Marines' presence violated the Posse Comitatus Act, which bars the military from domestic law enforcement. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals partially reversed. The administration deployed up to 4,000 National Guard personnel and relied on legal theories of implied presidential protective power for the Marines. Legal scholars described it as the most aggressive domestic military deployment against civilian protesters in decades.

title: Trump Coerces States with Federal Funding Tied to Policy Compliance
synopsis: Beginning in early 2025 and escalating through August 2025, the Trump administration and DOGE systematically attached unprecedented conditions to federal grants and withheld congressionally appropriated funds to coerce states into compliance with immigration enforcement, DEI elimination, and other White House priorities. In February 2025, the Education Department and DOGE gave states 14 days to eliminate all DEI programs or face funding revocation. DOGE employees seized control of Grants.gov and inserted new approval layers, blocking NIH from publishing normal funding opportunities — only three NOFOs between January 20 and March 26, 2025, compared to 163 in 2023. On August 7, 2025, Trump signed an executive order inserting political appointees into all federal grant review processes. Courts repeatedly blocked these conditions as violating the Constitution's Spending Clause. More than 30 local governments won a federal injunction in April 2025 blocking conditions on $4 billion in federal grants.

title: Trump DOJ Weaponized Against Political Opponents Including Comey, James, Cuomo
synopsis: By September 2025, Trump's Justice Department had opened or escalated criminal investigations against a sweeping list of political opponents including former FBI Director James Comey (indicted September 26, 2025 for allegedly lying to Congress), New York Attorney General Letitia James (grand jury convened investigating her civil fraud cases against Trump and the NRA), former Governor Andrew Cuomo, former national security adviser John Bolton, and Representative LaMonica McIver (D-NJ). Trump publicly pressured Attorney General Pam Bondi via social media to accelerate prosecutions. Georgetown law professor Paul Butler described the department as simultaneously deprioritizing fighting public corruption while weaponizing the DOJ against people Trump doesn't like. Former prosecutors noted Trump's former personal attorneys now occupied key positions and had fired dozens of career prosecutors. A September 2025 AP analysis found the DOJ had also classified liberal activist groups as potential domestic terrorist organizations. Legal experts described the pattern as unprecedented since Nixon.

title: Trump Repeatedly Floats Unconstitutional Third Presidential Term
synopsis: Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, Trump repeatedly and publicly entertained the idea of serving a third presidential term, directly contrary to the 22nd Amendment, which explicitly bars election to the presidency more than twice. In February 2026, at a Texas event, Trump told the crowd, Maybe we do one more term. Should we do one more? We're entitled to it because they cheated hell in the second one. The White House sold $50 Trump 2028 hats. Trump aides and allies including Steve Bannon and Stephen Miller openly discussed legal theories for circumventing the amendment — including a scheme whereby Trump would run as vice president, the president would resign, and Trump would assume the presidency by succession. Constitutional law professors across the political spectrum stated there were no credible legal arguments for a third term. On October 28, 2025, Trump said he was not allowed to run but had not definitively closed the door. House Speaker Mike Johnson said there was no path to amend the Constitution for a third Trump term.

title: Trump Threatens Criminal Prosecution of Election Officials Who Ran 2020 Election
synopsis: In a March 14, 2025 speech, Trump declared that election officials who administered the 2020 election should go to jail. The Brennan Center for Justice documented that the Trump administration built an infrastructure of DOJ task forces and working groups targeting election officials who had certified 2020 results. Trump signed an executive order directing the DOJ to review the actions of Chris Krebs — whom Trump himself had appointed to lead the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency — because Krebs had publicly stated the 2020 election was secure. By July 2025, the New York Times reported that senior DOJ officials were exploring whether to bring criminal charges against state and local election officials if they did not sufficiently safeguard election computer systems, based not on new evidence but on unsubstantiated fraud claims. Trump also publicly ordered the DOJ to intervene to free convicted election saboteur Tina Peters, calling her an innocent Political Prisoner, signaling that officials who had assisted his election subversion efforts would be protected.

title: National Guard Deployed to Chicago and Portland Over Democratic Governors Objections
synopsis: From September through November 2025, Trump dispatched National Guard troops to Chicago and Portland over the explicit objections of Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker and Oregon Governor Tina Kotek, framing anti-ICE protests in both cities as criminal insurrection. In October 2025, Trump threatened to invoke the Insurrection Act to sidestep court orders blocking the deployments. Hundreds of Texas National Guard soldiers gathered near Chicago while a federal judge had temporarily barred troops from Portland. Illinois Governor Pritzker accused Trump of using troops as a political tool and filed suit. NBC News reported in October 2025 that White House discussions had shifted from whether to invoke the Insurrection Act to how and when. Stephen Miller described the anti-ICE protests as an all-out campaign of insurrection against the sovereignty of the United States. The Supreme Court had not yet ruled on the legal boundaries. Legal experts warned that invoking the Insurrection Act against peaceful protesters would mark an unprecedented authoritarian escalation.

title: Venezuelan Deportees Tortured at El Salvador CECOT Prison
synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to deport 252 Venezuelan men to El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) without individual hearings. A November 2025 Human Rights Watch and Cristosal joint report titled Welcome to Hell, based on interviews with 40 of the 252 deportees, documented systematic torture including beatings, forced stress positions requiring 24-hour kneeling, solitary confinement, sexual assault by guards, food and medicine deprivation, and lights-on 24/7. ICE's own records showed only 3% of the men had been sentenced for violent crimes; HRW cross-referencing all 50 states found nearly half had no criminal history at all. Deportee Luis Munoz Pinto, a 27-year-old college student who had entered through the legal CBP One program, spent four months in CECOT. He told 60 Minutes: When you get there, you already know you're in hell. The $4.7 million deal with El Salvador gave the U.S. no accountability over conditions. Federal Judge James Boasberg ruled in June 2025 that the men had been plainly deprived of due process rights.

title: 52 Deaths in ICE Detention: Mortality Rate Highest in 20 Years
synopsis: Between January 20, 2025 and June 4, 2026, 52 people died in ICE custody — the highest mortality rate in over two decades and more than double Trump's first term rate, according to a June 2026 Human Rights Watch report titled Dying in Detention. The death rate was nearly four times that of the Biden administration. The Trump administration pushed ICE detention to a record high of 71,000 people by January 2026, up 77% from January 2025, while the annual death rate tripled — a disproportionate increase. In facilities where deaths occurred, populations were on average 242 detainees higher than the 10-year average in the two weeks before each death. Notable cases include Maksym Chernyak, 44, whose detention staff failed to call emergency services for over four and a half hours during a life-threatening emergency. A CNN investigation found many deaths were preventable due to understaffed medical teams, uninterrupted delays in offsite care, and DHS contractor failures. Deaths in 2026 were on track to exceed 2025.

title: Camp East Montana: Beatings, Medical Neglect, Deaths at Fort Bliss ICE Camp
synopsis: Camp East Montana, a sprawling ICE detention facility opened in August 2025 on Fort Bliss Army base in El Paso, Texas, became the subject of a devastating 84-page joint report by Human Rights Watch and the ACLU released in July 2026. Of 71 detainees interviewed over five months, approximately 90% — 64 individuals — said they had personally been assaulted by staff or witnessed others being beaten. Detainees reported being denied necessary medical care, forced to live in filthy conditions, and fed inedible meals. They were prevented from contacting lawyers or family members. Three detainees died at the facility in little more than six months, including a 55-year-old Cuban migrant who died in January 2026 after being held down by guards — and evidence in that death was missing or destroyed, per a Government Accountability Office report released June 2026. The GAO found significant, pervasive issues with planning, oversight, missing use-of-force reports, failure to administer medicine to seriously ill detainees, and tens of millions in wasted taxpayer funds through rushed contracts.

title: US Citizen Children Deported: 4-Year-Old Cancer Patient Sent to Honduras Without Medication
synopsis: In a pattern of unconstitutional deportations of American citizens documented by NY Magazine, multiple U.S.-born children were deported alongside undocumented parents in 2025. The most alarming case involved two U.S. citizen children — a 4-year-old boy with Stage 4 rare cancer and his 7-year-old sister — who were detained by ICE in El Paso and flown to Honduras before attorneys could file a habeas corpus petition. The boy was sent without his cancer medication and without opportunity to speak to lawyers, according to the National Immigration Project attorney Gracie Willis. Separately, a 2-year-old U.S. citizen girl was deported to Honduras on April 25 after her mother and sister attended a routine ISAP check-in on April 22. A 10-year-old U.S. citizen girl recovering from brain surgery was detained at a Border Patrol checkpoint in Texas on February 3 while her family was driving her to a Houston hospital appointment; despite a hospital letter, CBP detained the family for six hours and deported them to Mexico. DHS maintained: We don't have data to provide you on the deportation of U.S. citizens because we don't deport U.S. citizens.

title: Family Separation 2.0: Over 100,000 US Citizen Children Separated from Detained Parents
synopsis: A May 2026 Brookings Institution report estimated that more than 100,000 U.S. citizen children had a parent detained since Trump's mass deportation campaign began in January 2025, out of approximately 400,000 total immigration detentions. ProPublica found at least 11,000 American children had a parent detained in just the first seven months of Trump's second term — with Trump deporting roughly four times as many mothers of American children per day as Biden. Unlike Trump's first-term border separation policy, the new separations were more dispersed and hidden, occurring inside the U.S. during interior enforcement sweeps. In a documented case, a Russian asylum-seeking couple were told to deport to Russia or have their 8-year-old son placed in a government shelter; when they refused, ICE officers in May conducted interior separation and took the boy away at Kennedy International Airport. The Trump administration stripped the word humane from its Parental Interests Directive, renaming it the Detained Parents Directive and removing guidance requiring agents to handle immigrant parents humanely.

title: Mahmoud Khalil Detained for Pro-Palestinian Speech on Valid Green Card
synopsis: On March 8, 2025, ICE agents arrested Mahmoud Khalil, a 30-year-old Palestinian Columbia University graduate student with a valid green card, at his home in New York City. Khalil had participated in campus pro-Palestinian protests and served as a protest negotiator during the 2024 Gaza demonstrations; he had never been charged with a crime. His wife was eight months pregnant with their first child. The Trump administration cited a rarely invoked statute allowing the Secretary of State to expel noncitizens whose presence threatens U.S. foreign policy, alleging without evidence that Khalil had distributed pro-Hamas materials and failed to disclose UNRWA internship work on his green card application. UNRWA confirmed Khalil was an unpaid intern, never staff. Trump declared on Truth Social: This is the first arrest of many to come. Secretary of State Rubio said at a March 27 press conference that at least 300 international students had their visas revoked. A judge blocked Khalil's deportation on March 10, and he remained in a Louisiana detention facility as of late March 2025 — detained solely for his political speech.

title: Rumeysa Ozturk: Turkish PhD Student Secretly Moved to Louisiana for Co-Authoring Op-Ed
synopsis: On March 25, 2025, masked plainclothes ICE agents detained Rumeysa Ozturk, a 30-year-old Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University, as she walked near her home in Somerville, Massachusetts. Video of the arrest spread widely. Her sole apparent offense: co-authoring a student newspaper op-ed supporting Palestinian rights. DHS claimed without evidence that she had engaged in activities in support of Hamas. After her attorney filed a petition to keep her in Massachusetts, ICE secretly transferred her to Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center — notorious per the ACLU for a culture of abuse and unsanitary conditions — before a judge could rule on her case. A Massachusetts federal judge ordered March 28 that she could not be deported without a court order. Ozturk was among the targets of the Trump administration's campaign to detain and deport visa-holding foreign students involved in pro-Palestinian activism. A federal judge ruled in September 2025 that government officials deliberately and with purposeful aforethought coordinated two federal agencies to intentionally chill the rights to freedom of speech of Middle Eastern studies scholars.

title: US Citizens Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez and Jose Hermosillo Detained by ICE Despite Documentation
synopsis: A documented pattern of ICE detaining American citizens swept through 2025. Juan Carlos Lopez-Gomez, 20, born in Georgia, was arrested on April 16 during a traffic stop in Florida under a state law that a federal judge had already suspended on April 4. He presented his Social Security card and Georgia REAL ID to police but was held for more than 30 hours. ICE placed a detainer on the jail even after a judge found no probable cause. DHS falsely claimed Lopez-Gomez had identified himself as undocumented. Jose Hermosillo, 19, of Albuquerque, was arrested by Border Patrol in Tucson on April 9 while visiting with his girlfriend — 70 miles from the Mexican border — and held for 10 days before his family secured his release by providing proof of citizenship. DHS alleged Hermosillo told an agent he was born in Mexico; Hermosillo denied it, and attorneys noted he has a learning disability. In May 2026, a top ICE official stated at a border security conference: Since the start of this administration, we have not had any arrests of U.S. citizens... That's happened zero times — a claim directly contradicted by available evidence.

title: Leo Garcia Venegas: US Citizen Detained Three Times in ICE Racial Profiling Stops
synopsis: Leo Garcia Venegas, a U.S. citizen and Alabama construction worker, was detained by immigration agents three separate times through May 2026. The first incident in mid-2025 involved agents tackling him while he filmed his brother's arrest at a construction site, ignoring his citizenship claims. A few weeks later, an officer at a home he was building refused to trust his Alabama REAL ID — which only citizens and legal residents can obtain. Videos went viral; Garcia Venegas testified before Congress and filed a federal lawsuit. Despite the pending lawsuit, he was detained a third time in May 2026. The same week, masked agents in the Bronx tackled an American teenager who, once identified as a citizen, was left bloody and bruised in an unfamiliar neighborhood. ProPublica reported that in response to its coverage, ICE official Todd Lyons acknowledged citizen detentions serve as a deterrent. His attorney argued the stops constitute racial profiling stops based on the Supreme Court's fall 2024 ruling permitting stops partly based on apparent ethnicity, job in construction, and speaking Spanish. Despite three documented detentions, ICE denied his damage claim in April 2026 with no explanation, then detained him again two weeks later.

title: Alien Enemies Act Deportations: 137 Venezuelans Sent to CECOT Without Any Due Process
synopsis: On March 15–16, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act — not used since World War II — to deport 137 Venezuelan nationals to El Salvador's CECOT prison with no notice, no hearings, and no opportunity to challenge removal. Federal Judge James Boasberg had issued a temporary restraining order blocking deportation flights, and evidence emerged that planes carrying detainees had been ordered to continue to El Salvador even after the TRO was issued. In June 2025, Boasberg ruled in a sweeping opinion that the men had been plainly deprived of due process rights, comparing their situation to a Kafka novel: Perhaps the President lawfully invoked the Alien Enemies Act. Perhaps, moreover, Defendants are correct that Plaintiffs are gang members. But there is simply no way to know for sure, as the CECOT Plaintiffs never had any opportunity to challenge the Government's say-so. The Supreme Court unanimously agreed the men were entitled to notice and the opportunity to challenge removal before deportation. The administration had given some detainees as little as 24 hours notice.

title: Muslim Organizations Stripped of Security Grants by DHS Amid Rising Mosque Attacks
synopsis: Beginning in spring 2025, Trump's Department of Homeland Security stripped dozens of Muslim organizations of eligibility for FEMA's Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP), using vague terrorism allegations without supporting evidence, CNN reported in October 2025. DHS proposed a blanket ban on Muslim organizations receiving security grants. The Islamic Society of North America, which had received $150,000 for security upgrades during Biden's term, was rejected. New NSGP terms required recipients to cooperate with immigration enforcement, ban DEI programs, and avoid boycott advocacy. This occurred as mosque attacks surged: in May 2026, two teenage shooters attacked the Islamic Center of San Diego, killing security guard Amin Abdullah and two others. CAIR's 2026 Civil Rights Report documented 8,683 complaints in 2025 — the highest since 1996 — with a 96% increase in Minnesota and 65% in Illinois. CAIR documented 33 incidents explicitly targeting Islamic institutions. DNI Tulsi Gabbard in December 2025 claimed American Muslims were working to impose sharia law through use of laws or violence, naming specific cities as examples.

title: Green Card Holders Detained for Decades-Old Minor Crimes; LPRs Fear Leaving US
synopsis: Under Trump's second term, Customs and Border Protection and ICE sharply escalated enforcement against lawful permanent residents upon reentry, targeting people with decades-old criminal records that had previously been overlooked. Lewelyn Dixon, a 64-year-old Filipina legal permanent resident, was arrested at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and held for nearly three months after she disclosed a past workplace theft conviction from years prior, despite having lived blamelessly in her American community since. Her attorney noted he had handled three similar cases since February 2025 alone — unprecedented in his 12-year career. The pattern extended to Green Card holders with minor resolved records facing surprise detention when attempting to re-enter from international travel. Yunseo Chung, a 21-year-old Korean American Columbia University student who had lived in the U.S. since age seven as a lawful permanent resident, had her LPR status revocation initiated by DHS over pro-Palestinian protest participation. A federal judge ruled on March 25, 2025 that Chung could not be detained while fighting the revocation. Immigration attorneys reported a flood of clients asking whether they could safely leave the country at all — a chilling effect on the freedom of movement of 13 million legal permanent residents.

title: Transgender Military Ban: Thousands of Troops Discharged for Gender Identity
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, President Trump signed Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness, an executive order reinstating the transgender military ban and directing the discharge of all transgender service members. The order declared that expressing a false gender identity divergent from an individual's sex cannot satisfy the rigorous standards necessary for military service. The order revoked Biden's Executive Order 14004, which had allowed transgender service members to serve openly and receive transition-related care. A federal judge initially blocked the ban as unconstitutional, but on May 6, 2025, the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority allowed the ban to take effect while legal challenges continued — clearing the way for thousands of transgender troops to be discharged. The Department of Defense was directed within 60 days to update medical standards to bar those with gender dysphoria, end invented and identification-based pronoun usage, and prohibit shared facilities based on gender identity. Simultaneously, the State Department suspended all passport applications requesting sex-marker changes, and the administration issued a government-wide executive order declaring the U.S. government recognizes only two sexes.

title: CISA Election Security Team Placed on Leave, Dismantled
synopsis: Beginning February 7, 2025, the Trump administration placed at least 17 staffers from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Election Security and Resilience team on administrative leave, pending a review focused on anti-disinformation activities. Within weeks, more than 130 CISA employees overall were fired, including 10 regional specialists who liaised directly with state and local election offices. Acting CISA director Bridget Bean issued a Valentine's Day memo defunding the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center (EI-ISAC), a nationwide program providing threat monitoring to state election officials. The memo ordered a review of every election security position and program dating back to Trump's first term. Attorney General Pam Bondi on February 5 separately disbanded the FBI task force on election threats against election workers. Democrats on the Senate and House oversight committees warned the moves left states without federal protection against ransomware and foreign cyberattacks ahead of the 2026 midterms. Former officials said the cuts specifically targeted staff who had monitored Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence operations in the 2024 election cycle.

title: AG Bondi Disbands FBI Foreign Influence Task Force on Day One
synopsis: On her first day in office, February 5, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a policy memo disbanding the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, a unit of approximately 50 agents and support staff established in 2017 to investigate and disrupt covert foreign interference in U.S. elections. The memo also drastically narrowed enforcement of the Foreign Agents Registration Act, limiting criminal charges to conduct similar to traditional espionage. Bondi simultaneously disbanded Task Force Klepto Capture and the Kleptocracy Asset Recovery Initiative targeting Russian oligarch assets. The Foreign Influence Task Force had previously exposed a Russia-backed scheme that funneled $10 million to conservative U.S. media companies and regularly briefed social media platforms about disinformation campaigns from Russia, China, and Iran. Former counterintelligence chief David Laufman said the order raised serious questions about Bondi's commitment to combating foreign influence operations. Critics noted the timing coincided with Trump's ongoing false claims about the 2020 election and came months before the 2026 midterm elections when foreign adversaries could exploit the resulting intelligence gap.

title: DOGE-SSA Employees Sign Secret Voter Data Agreement with True the Vote
synopsis: In March 2025, two DOGE staffers embedded at the Social Security Administration were contacted by a political advocacy group widely identified as True the Vote seeking to analyze state voter rolls using SSA data to find evidence of voter fraud and to overturn election results in certain States. One DOGE staffer signed a Voter Data Agreement on March 24, 2025, in his capacity as an SSA employee without the knowledge or approval of SSA leadership or review through proper data exchange procedures. The arrangement was not discovered until November 2025, when an internal SSA audit uncovered it. The SSA made two Hatch Act referrals to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel in late December 2025. The Trump administration admitted to these facts in a January 16, 2026, court filing in a lawsuit by the AFL-CIO. Separately, DOGE staff shared SSA data through an unapproved third-party Cloudflare server and transmitted a password-protected file containing personal information on roughly 1,000 individuals to senior DOGE adviser Steve Davis. SSA whistleblower Charles Borges alleged that DOGE staffers also copied a dataset of more than 300 million Americans' information into an unsecured cloud server.

title: Trump Attempts to Illegally Fire FEC Chair Ellen Weintraub
synopsis: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Chair Ellen Weintraub — a Democratic commissioner who had been an outspoken critic of Trump's campaign finance violations — stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub publicly rejected the removal as illegal, noting that no president had ever fired an FEC commissioner and that the Federal Election Campaign Act contained no firing authority for the president. Republican former FEC Chair Trevor Potter called the action contrary to law, noting that Trump was free to nominate a replacement but could not simply fire a sitting commissioner. The timing was significant: the FEC was preparing to consider complaints against Trump's 2024 campaign and against Elon Musk's $277 million in political spending. Weintraub lost her email, computer, and cellphone access by February 7. The move was part of a broader pattern of firing independent agency members and preceded the eventual July 2026 Supreme Court ruling that gave presidents expanded power to fire independent agency members.

title: DOJ Sues 30+ States Demanding Detailed Voter Registration Databases
synopsis: Beginning in mid-2025 and escalating through 2026, the Department of Justice launched an unprecedented campaign to compel all 50 states and the District of Columbia to turn over detailed voter registration databases containing voters' full names, dates of birth, residential addresses, driver's license numbers, and last four digits of Social Security numbers. The DOJ pursued this under a confidential memorandum of understanding framework citing EO 14248. By May 2026, the DOJ had filed lawsuits against 30 states and D.C. that refused. By July 2026, courts had ruled against the DOJ in all 16 federal court decisions issued on the matter, with a Rhode Island judge calling it a fishing expedition and seven of the 15 district court judges who ruled against Trump having been appointed by Trump himself. Even Republican-controlled states including Idaho, Utah, West Virginia, and Kentucky resisted, citing privacy concerns. Critics warned the consolidated database would create a federal surveillance tool over American voters. Democratic states described it as an attempt to nationalize elections in violation of the Constitution's elections clause.

title: FBI Seizes 700 Boxes of 2020 Fulton County Georgia Ballots
synopsis: On January 28, 2026 — one week after Trump publicly predicted prosecutions over the 2020 election — FBI agents executed a search warrant at Fulton County's Elections Hub and Operations Center in Union City, Georgia, loading hundreds of boxes of sealed 2020 election ballots, tabulator tapes, ballot images, and voter rolls into trucks. Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin reported the FBI sought approximately 700 boxes. The warrant alleged possible violations of federal record-retention and election-integrity statutes, though election experts noted no new evidence of fraud had emerged. Fulton County Commissioner Marvin Arrington called it an unprecedented breach of chain of custody. A federal court denied the county's motion to return the seized materials. The seizure occurred months after a Georgia prosecutor dropped the 2023 state-level election interference case against Trump and 18 co-defendants. The Congressional Research Service noted the seizure was legally unprecedented, characterizing it as the first known instance of federal agents physically seizing sealed election ballots from a certified election.

title: DOJ Threatens Criminal Charges Against State Election Officials Over Voter Rolls
synopsis: On July 7, 2026, with the November midterms less than four months away, the DOJ Civil Rights Division sent letters to election officials in all 50 states and D.C. warning that they could face criminal charges if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to vote or remain on voter rolls, demanding a response within five days on intended compliance. The letters invoked statutes carrying prison sentences for election officials found to have issued ballots to ineligible voters. Senior DOJ officials had been exploring criminal charges against state election officials as early as July 2025 — not based on new evidence but on ideological pressure. UCLA law professor Rick Hasen described the letters as Trump trying to use whatever levers of power and persuasive power to interfere with how states run the 2026 election. Separately, a federal judge blocked a DOJ grand jury subpoena seeking the names and contact information of every Georgia election worker from the 2020 election, calling the subpoena's breadth staggering.

title: Trump Fires All Three Election Assistance Commission Members Before Midterms
synopsis: On July 9, 2026 — less than four months before the November midterms — President Trump fired all three remaining members of the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission, leaving the federal agency that certifies voting systems, distributes election security grants, and maintains the national voter registration form without any commissioners. Democratic commissioners Thomas Hicks and Benjamin W. Hovland received brief termination emails from White House aide Morgan DeWitt Snow. Republican commissioner Christy McCormick was pressured to resign. A fourth commissioner, Republican Don Palmer, had already resigned in April for a Heritage Foundation post. The White House justified the firings by citing the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling expanding presidential authority to remove independent agency members. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it a brazen attempt to seize control of our elections before a single vote is cast. With CISA already gutted, the EAC was one of the few remaining federal entities providing election security support to states.

title: Trump Primetime Address Spreads Election Disinformation Before 2026 Midterms
synopsis: On July 16, 2026, President Trump delivered a nationally televised primetime address alleging shocking vulnerabilities in American elections and claiming China had conducted the largest compromise of election data in history by acquiring 220 million voter registration files. The White House released a cache of declassified documents but a White House official admitted before the speech that none of it would show votes were switched or machines hacked. FactCheck.org, the Associated Press, and CBS News found the address contained numerous misleading claims. Intelligence officials noted the 2021 U.S. National Intelligence Council had assessed with high confidence that China did not interfere in the 2020 election. Trump claimed voting machines were extremely exposed to attack while citing Venezuela-related intelligence about Smartmatic — a company not used in U.S. elections outside Los Angeles County. Election security expert David Becker said after 18 months and untold taxpayer resources, the administration had found only rehashed, debunked conspiracy theories.

title: DHS Secretary Mullin Threatens States with Investigations Over Voter Roll Compliance
synopsis: On July 17, 2026 — one day after Trump's primetime election address — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a White House press conference warning that states could lose federal funding or face federal investigations if they failed to comply with the administration's election security demands, including running voter rolls through the SAVE citizenship verification database. Mullin pledged to aggressively monitor public voter lists to pursue voter fraud cases before and after the November election. The threats came as the administration was already losing all 16 court rulings on its voter roll demands and as the SAVE database had just been blocked by a federal judge. UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen called the threats likely hollow given the courts had blocked the underlying initiatives, but warned the statements would further doubts about election processes and create headaches for states preparing for November. Mullin's remarks compounded the chilling effect created by the DOJ's July 7 letters threatening criminal charges against election officials.

title: Mass Firing of 18 Independent Inspectors General
synopsis: On the night of January 24-25, 2025, the Trump administration fired 18 independent inspectors general across federal agencies including Defense, State, Transportation, Agriculture, Commerce, Health and Human Services, and Education. The dismissals violated the 2022 Inspector General Reform Act, which requires 30 days written notice to Congress with substantive justification before an IG can be removed. No such notice was given. Hannibal Mike Ware, head of the Council of Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency, was among those fired and confirmed the number. Sen. Chuck Grassley, Republican chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, stated the firings did not comply with the law. Legal experts and oversight advocates said the purge was designed to eliminate independent watchdogs and replace them with loyalists, removing the last internal checks on corruption within each agency. Sen. Elizabeth Warren called it a purge of independent watchdogs in the middle of the night.

title: DOJ Fires 17+ Career Prosecutors Who Investigated Trump
synopsis: On January 27, 2025, the Trump Justice Department fired more than 17 career prosecutors who had worked on special counsel Jack Smith's investigations of Trump, including Molly Gaston, J.P. Cooney, Anne McNamara, and Mary Dohrmann. The termination letters explicitly cited their roles in prosecuting Trump as the reason, stating You played a significant role in prosecuting President Trump and that leadership cannot trust you. In the preceding days, senior career officials overseeing national security, public corruption, antitrust, and environmental law were reassigned to areas outside their expertise, including a sanctuary cities task force. George Toscas, who oversaw the FBI search of Mar-a-Lago, was among those reassigned. Five former DOJ and FBI officials told NBC News the firings were designed to intimidate the workforce and deter future investigations of the Trump administration. Legal experts called it retribution and behavior modification through fear.
